subject: physics
question_text: Why is it easier to perform the skating on the snow?

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2017 (Q8) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section A, 2 marks. appearances[] is left empty deliberately: a separate reviewed tagging pass fills that field from a reviewed mapping, so a hand-written entry here would read as an invented tag. The 1+1 split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked against the board's marked answer: P = F/A, so the same weight on the very small contact area of the blade gives a large pressure; a large pressure lowers the melting point of ice; a thin film of water forms under the blade and acts as a lubricant, so friction is small. The marked answer is written as the board states it. The second step's `why` records, without altering the marked answer, that modern measurements attribute the film to frictional heating and to a liquid-like surface layer on ice as well as to pressure.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The pressure is large
lines: The skate blade touches the snow over a
very small area, so the pressure under it

lines.text: P = F/A,  small A gives large P

steps.margin_note: First mark. Small contact area, large pressure. Write P = F/A.
steps.why: Pressure is force divided by area. The skater's weight does not change, so the small contact area of the blade edge is the only reason the pressure is large.
common_mistakes: Saying the skater weighs less on snow. The weight is the same; only the contact area is small.

recall.must_convey: That the blade has a very small contact area, so the pressure under it is large.

steps.memory_tip: Same weight, much smaller area. P = F/A makes the pressure under the blade large.

steps.label: The water film lubricates
lines: A large pressure lowers the melting point
of ice. A thin film of water forms under
the blade and acts as a lubricant.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the water film and call it a lubricant.
steps.why: The marked answer runs through the melting point of ice: a large pressure lowers it, a thin water film forms and lubricates the blade, so the friction is small. Modern measurements show that heating from the sliding itself, and a liquid-like layer already present on the ice surface, also add to that film.
common_mistakes: Stopping at "the pressure is large" without saying what the pressure does to the ice.
Calling the water film a result of warm air rather than of the pressure.

recall.must_convey: That the large pressure lowers the melting point of ice, a thin water film forms, and that film acts as a lubricant so friction is small.
accept: the film acts as a lubricant
water film lubricant la pani chestundi

steps.memory_tip: Pressure up, melting point down, water film, friction small. Four links in that order.

insider_note: Two marks, two links: the large pressure, then the water film that lowers the friction. Naming only the pressure earns one of the two.
